articles.title: In 2025, UAE researchers placed two solar panels back to back with mist cooling between them; outdoor tests produced 26% more energy than a standard uncooled panel
articles.summary: In 2025, researchers from UAE University and the University of Sharjah discovered an innovative method to enhance solar panel efficiency by 26.05% using mist cooling technology between bifacial panels. This breakthrough could significantly boost energy generation in hot climates, paving the way for more sustainable solar energy solutions.
articles.body: After a few hours in the sun, a solar panel can feel hot to the touch. The fuel is sunlight, but the heat it brings with it quietly erodes the panel’s output. Engineers cannot overlook that heat penalty in a country like the United Arab Emirates, where rooftops and desert solar farms bake for most of the year. Usable space is also limited, especially on rooftops, and cooling devices that waste energy or water can quickly offset any savings.Researchers from United Arab Emirates University and the University of Sharjah tackled both difficulties at once. In 2025, they reported that two solar panels placed back to back with a fine spray of water between them produced 26.05% more energy in outdoor tests than a standard single-sided panel with no cooling. The design is called a mist-cooled sandwich bifacial panel, and the aim is to get more electricity out of the same area while keeping the panels cooler.Why heat hurts solar outputSolar panels are rated at 25°C, but a panel sitting in direct desert sun can run far hotter than that. Silicon cells lose efficiency as they warm up, and researchers have studied the effect for decades. A 1996 survey by scientists at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory looked at how cells, modules and complete systems respond to temperature, and other researchers have cited it widely ever since. Published measurements for silicon modules usually land between 0.25% and 0.5% of power lost for every degree above the rating temperature. That sounds tiny until the maths is done. A module running 35 degrees above its 25°C rating and losing 0.4% of its power per degree would lose 14% of its rated output. Spread across thousands of panels and a long hot summer, the loss becomes real money.Bifacial panels are good at wringing out extra energy because they capture light on both sides, including sunlight bouncing up from the ground. They run hot, too. The UAE team’s twist was to create the bifacial effect by mounting two standard single-sided panels back to back and cooling the gap between them. Each panel was a 60 W monocrystalline unit, and the mist system used 16 nozzles behind the front panel and 16 behind the back one, according to PV Magazine.What the field test demonstratedThe tests were conducted outdoors in the extreme heat of the UAE. The results were published in July 2025 by Zafar Said and Fahad Faraz Ahmad in the journal Energy Conversion and Management. The sandwich panel generated 26.05% more energy than a standard monofacial panel, the type that collects light only from the front, running without cooling.The mist also kept the cells cooler, which is where the higher numbers come from. Corresponding author Zafar Said told PV Magazine that in extremely hot conditions the mist-cooled sandwich panels generated up to 37% more electricity on sunny days and up to 46% more on cloudy days than standard single-sided panels. These are best-case daily gains, while the study’s headline result is the 26.05% gain in energy yield. The larger cloudy-day figure is a little surprising, and the published summary does not explain it, so the full paper should be read before drawing conclusions. Stretched over a whole year, the team calculated that the system would deliver 45.34 kWh more per square metre than a single-sided setup. That works out to an annual gain of about $5.48 per square metre.Water and scaling problemsIn a desert environment, the most obvious problem is water. It is vital for mist cooling, and the UAE has little to spare. Said the next steps involve fine-tuning the mist system to reduce both water and energy use, and testing second-life solar panels inside the sandwich design for improved sustainability. He added that the technique has been patented.Another open question is scale. The prototype used two 60 W panels, which is minuscule next to a utility solar farm, and all the numbers come from a single climate. The annual gain of $5.48 per square metre is small, so the cost of pumps, nozzles, piping and water would have to stay comfortably below it for the idea to make commercial sense. The open question is whether the concept survives real-world water prices and broader testing. If it does, hot countries could get more power from the solar sites they already have, rather than needing to build more of them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: France's world famous Louvre Museum in Paris was temporarily closed on Monday soon after protesters supporting a student movement blocked access to the museum.In a message to visitors, the museum said it was closed for the time being due to a student social movement and strikes. It apologised for the inconvenience caused. "Dear visitors, due to a student social movement, the museum is closed for the time being. We apologize for the inconvenience caused," it said on X.The museum did not provide further details about when it would reopen.This mueseum also became widely discussed place, as exactly one year ago, it became a target in high-value heist. In the daylight robbery, thieves used a vehicle-mounted ladder to enter the museum's Apollo Gallery through a window and stole eight pieces of historic French royal jewellery, including tiaras, necklaces and brooches, in less than eight minutes. The stolen jewels were valued at approximately 88 million euros ($102 million). The robbery raised serious concerns over security at one of the world's most visited museums.Meanwhile, the current closure comes as France grapples with widespread protests, started September, initially sparked by student anger over teacher shortages, poor school infrastructure and deteriorating education standards. The movement has since expanded into nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services. Over half a million people took to the streets on Saturday, with protests turning violent in several cities, including Paris, Marseille and Lyon, leading to widespread arrests and clashes with police.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2004, Missouri rebuilt 2.36 miles of deteriorating roads with recycled asphalt and fly ash; an EPA estimate put the project’s cost at about one-third less than full replacement
articles.summary: Discover how Jackson County, Missouri, transformed 2.36 miles of deteriorating roads using recycled asphalt and coal fly ash to reduce costs by a third and promote sustainability in highway construction.
articles.body: It may be necessary to remove the old pavement, remove the debris, and install new materials in order to replace a severely degraded road. An alternative strategy was attempted by engineers in Jackson County, Missouri. The road itself was repurposed, and the ground pavement was combined with water and coal fly ash to create a new base for an asphalt surface. The project covered 2.36 miles of rural roads and used nearly 1,700 U.S. tons of Class C fly ash, a byproduct of coal-fired power generation. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s case study documents the project’s length, donated materials and reported cost savings.The project was conducted in partnership with Jackson County’s Department of Public Works, Kansas City Power & Light, Lafarge North America and the University of Missouri–Kansas City. It was a realistic test of whether an existing pavement could be used as a structural layer or if it was viewed as material to be scrapped.Old path to new baseThis is called full-depth cold in-place recycling. Rather than tear out the old asphalt and transport it to a processing factory, crews pulverise the current pavement and underlying base material in place. The recovered mixture is then processed, compressed and overlaid with a fresh surface course. For the Jackson County project, engineers employed Class C fly ash, which is self-cementing. The addition of this sort of ash to water might cause binding reactions that assist in stabilising granular material. Combined with the crushed asphalt and base material, it produced a more durable basis for the new surface.The process also affected the amount of material that had to be added to or removed from the road. The fly ash was used to stabilise the recycled base, and the old pavement was kept as part of the restored construction. Then, as a fresh asphalt layer, the finished driving surface was laid on top. In a 2008 technical paper, Anil Misra and coauthors described the Jackson County demonstration as an August 2004 project covering approximately 2.5 miles across two road segments. That is a rounded figure; the EPA lists the exact length as 2.36 miles. The study examined construction procedures, field strength tests and follow-up measurements to assess the performance of the fly ash-stabilised recycled base.What the strength tests revealedA recycled road base needs to look solid after compaction and be more than that. It must withstand frequent deformation by vehicles and variations in temperature and moisture. One of the tests utilised in the Missouri project was the California bearing ratio, or CBR. The test assesses the material’s resistance to penetration and aids engineers in determining appropriateness for pavement construction. The EPA case study reports that the fly ash-stabilised material reached an average California bearing ratio (CBR) of 52 after 24 to 48 hours of curing. That early strength allowed engineers to employ a thinner asphalt wearing surface, lowering the quantity of new pavement material required.The investigation did not end with the initial construction results. Engineers returned to the road sections and measured structural response using a falling-weight deflectometer. The device exerts a controlled stress on the pavement and measures the resulting deflection, which can provide information on the stiffness of the layers underneath. The follow-up work was conducted on two road sections, J.W. Cummins Road and Cummings Road. Researchers made many measurements along the pavement, at several points, so they could compare the structural behaviour at the different reconstructed parts, not just one measurement.Misra and his coauthors estimated structural layer coefficients of 0.18–0.26 for the stabilized base, above the 0.14 reference value for a typical granular base. They recommended a more conservative design range of 0.18–0.20 when calculating pavement thicknesses with the recycled material. Those statistics are important because the structural layer coefficient allows engineers to gauge the contribution of a pavement layer towards the strength of the entire highway. The results revealed that the recycled, fly ash-stabilised base might give considerable structural support, rather than simply compacted fill.Why the project was cheaperThe EPA attributed the project’s cost advantage to several factors. Crews processed the existing pavement on site, reducing the need to haul away old asphalt, transport replacement aggregate and dispose of waste in a landfill. Reusing the existing road material also reduced demand for newly quarried stone and sand.The project additionally used nearly 1,700 U.S. tons of Class C fly ash donated by Kansas City Power & Light and Lafarge North America. The stabilised base was strong enough to support a thinner, less expensive asphalt wearing surface. Because the fly ash was donated, the reported savings should not be attributed solely to the recycling method or assumed to apply to projects where equivalent materials must be purchased.There was also an environmental benefit in terms of fewer truck trips. Hauling old pavement away and hauling fresh aggregate to a construction site uses fuel and emits pollution. That activity was decreased by the reuse of material already on the road and limited the requirement for newly mined stone and sand. The one-third reduction was an estimate for this specific project, not a guaranteed saving for every road. Results can vary with pavement condition, ash composition, transport distances, equipment costs and the thickness of the replacement surface.Limits to reusing a roadThe Missouri test proved that recycled pavement and self-cementing fly ash could be blended into a viable base, but it did not eliminate the necessity for engineering checks. The existing road material had to be processable; the mixture had to have the right moisture, compaction and curing. Fly ash can also vary by source. The chemical composition of ash determines how it reacts with water and other materials; therefore, results from one project cannot be immediately transferred to every supply of coal ash. Engineers must determine the appropriate mix proportions and verify that the finished material meets the specifications for its intended use.Then there is long-term performance. Initial bearing strength and pavement stiffness measures assist in determining if a road can handle loads, but they are no substitute for years of monitoring under traffic and weather conditions. Design guidance was developed from the Missouri experiment, although the authors warn that field measurements and material attributes should be evaluated with care.The Jackson County project demonstrated an alternative to complete road replacement. Crews recycled 2.36 miles of deteriorating pavement, stabilised the reclaimed material with nearly 1,700 U.S. tons of Class C fly ash, and applied a new asphalt surface. The EPA reported that the project cost about one-third less than removing and replacing the entire road. The broader lesson is that worn pavement does not always need to be discarded. When the existing material is suitable and engineers design the mixture correctly, recycling and fly ash stabilisation can reduce the need for new materials, hauling and landfill disposal.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'O Captain, My Captain': Should Congress make room for Amarinder Singh again?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Can a party install a new captain, retain the old team and still leave the door open for a former captain who quit the dressing room five years
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Can a party install a new captain, retain the old team and still leave the door open for a former captain who quit the dressing room five years ago? With the leadership chanting 'O Captain! My Captain!' the Punjab Congress seems to be attempting to navigate that question precisely ahead of the 2027 assembly elections.With Pargat Singh at the helm, Raja Warring and Charanjit Singh Channi 'promised' an active role in the campaign; Sachin Pilot has also left the door open to Captain Amarinder Singh's possible return. Can Congress accommodate its old captain without unsettling the new captain and the team?Congress general secretary Sachin Pilot, the party's Punjab in-charge, on October 15 offered a line that will keep speculation alive: "Politics mein 'kuch bhi ho sakta hai' (anything is possible in politics)."Asked about the possibility of former Punjab chief minister Captain Amarinder Singh returning to Congress, Pilot praised him as a leader who had served Punjab "well" and was "a man of a very tall stature". He clarified, however, that he had not spoken to Captain Amarinder about his political plans."I've not spoken to him personally about what his future plans are about joining or leaving any party," Pilot told PTI Videos.The remark came less than a fortnight after Congress appointed former India hockey captain Pargat Singh as Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) president, replacing Amrinder Singh Raja Warring on October 2. It also followed Amarinder's public criticism of the BJP, the party he joined in 2022, over its handling of Punjab.So, is Congress merely acknowledging political speculation, or could the old captain's name return to the party's calculations? And if he does return, where would he fit in a state unit that has just changed leadership and is yet to name a CM face?The 'Uncle Amarinder' connectionThe latest speculation began with an unexpected public greeting. On August 6, during an Instagram 'Ask Me Anything' session with students, leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi was asked to name his favourite BJP politician."Captain Amarinder Singh, definitely. I get along with him, he's cool and he is an expert on military history, so I like him quite a lot," Rahul Gandhi said, before adding: "Hello, Uncle Amarinder!"The former CM responded that his personal relationship with the Gandhi family would remain, but his political commitment was to the BJP. In a September interview with The Tribune, he said he remained fond of Rahul, Priyanka and Sonia Gandhi, while distinguishing personal relationships from politics."My personal relationship with the Gandhis will always be there, but my political commitment is to the BJP," he said."If tomorrow I tell Rahul, Priyanka or Sonia personally that I'll be there for them no matter what, I mean it and I'm happy to help," he added.The indirect exchange was notable because Amarinder Singh's departure from Congress in September 2021 followed a bitter confrontation with the party's state leadership. "When you've been with somebody for fifty years, they remain your party. I never asked to leave them; they asked me to leave," Captain Amarinder Singh said recently.Amarinder's BJP discontentThe former chief minister's recent criticism of the BJP has provided the immediate backdrop to the comeback speculation.In an interview published by The Tribune on September 25, Amarinder said the BJP had not consulted him on Punjab politics or policy despite his long experience in the state."I haven't had a single meeting on Punjab policy or politics with them in the last five years," he said.He was more direct about his decision to join the party: "I have gained nothing by joining BJP."Amarinder also argued that the BJP did not adequately understand Punjab and should consult leaders familiar with the state's political and social realities. He advocated an alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal, pointing to the BJP's historical position as the junior partner in that relationship.In the same interview, he described himself as going through "difficult times", without elaborating.Yet he has also made clear that dissatisfaction does not automatically mean departure. Amarinder Singh said it was his duty to tell the BJP what he thought about Punjab and that criticising the party's approach did not mean he was quitting.From a 77-seat victory to a bitter exitCaptain Amarinder Singh's record in Congress spans decades, including two terms as Punjab CM, from 2002 to 2007 and from 2017 to 2021.In the 2017 assembly election, Congress won 77 of Punjab's 117 seats under his leadership, returning to power after a decade. But the relationship between Amarinder Singh and the state leadership deteriorated, particularly amid his prolonged confrontation with Navjot Singh Sidhu.Sidhu became Punjab Congress president in July 2021. The conflict intensified over leadership and the government's handling of election promises. On September 18, 2021, Amarinder resigned as chief minister after the Congress high command called a meeting of the party's legislators to discuss leadership.He subsequently left Congress and launched the Punjab Lok Congress (PLC). In the 2022 assembly election, the PLC allied with the BJP, but the alliance failed to win a seat for Amarinder Singh's party. AAP swept the election with 92 seats, while Congress was reduced to 18.Amarinder joined the BJP in September 2022, and his PLC was merged with it.The electoral record provides the context for the renewed speculation, but it does not establish that bringing Amarinder back would reverse Congress's fortunes. The party's 2022 defeat followed a wider political shift in Punjab, including AAP's rise and Congress's internal divisions.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Pargat Singh's leadership testMeanwhile, Pargat Singh's appointment has put a new leader at the head of a state unit that has repeatedly struggled with factional disputes. A former India hockey captain and three-time MLA from Jalandhar Cantonment, he was associated with Sidhu during the 2021 confrontation with Amarinder Singh and had publicly questioned the previous government's delivery on election promises.Pilot called Pargat a "unifying captain", saying the new president has reached out to state leaders and received public support. He has also invoked the team metaphor to describe Congress's approach to the election."You are one captain who's got a fantastic team, and the captain is only as strong as his team," Pilot said he had told Pargat. His appointment, replacing Warring as state chief, was particularly important in the backdrop of an internal tussle between Warring and Channi camps.Punjab Congress has spent months grappling with a bitter power struggle between the camps of state chief Amarinder Singh Raja Warring and former CM Charanjit Singh Channi. The feud spilled into public view through rival sloganeering, poster wars, clashes at party events and boycotts during visits by then state in-charge Bhupesh Baghel. The high command's July compromise, retaining Warring while appointing Channi to head the campaign committee, failed to end the friction. After Sachin Pilot replaced Baghel as Punjab in-charge in September, Warring eventually resigned on October 2, and Pargat Singh was appointed the new state chief.With the Congress leadership now sending the open-door signal to Captain Amarinder, the question is how Pargat's team would accommodate a strong-headed former CM with a history in the party.Moreover, the issue is not limited to Amarinder Singh. In the upcoming months, Congress must also manage the transition from Warring, who led the state unit from April 2022 until October 2026.No CM face, but several leadership questionsCongress has also decided against projecting a CM face for the 2027 Punjab election.Pilot said the party would fight as a team and decide who should lead the state after securing the mandate, following consultations with workers, leaders and MLAs."We are fighting together as a team. Let the team win. And then we'll decide who gets to do what job," he said.The party has several experienced leaders, including Partap Singh Bajwa, Sukhjinder Randhawa, Charanjit Singh Channi and Warring. Pargat's appointment adds a new organisational chief to that mix, while the question of Amarinder's possible return remains unconfirmed.For the high command, the practical issue would be defining the role of each leader without undermining the other.What could Captain Amarinder's return meanAmarinder Singh's long tenure in Punjab politics, his experience as CM and his association with national security and border-state issues are part of his public political profile. A return could give Congress another experienced voice in its campaign, while his criticism of the BJP could offer a new line of political debate. The Congress may gain from his name, polularity and political history but it is unlikely that he would have any active role owing to his age.But the political costs would depend on the terms of any return. His 2021 exit followed a major leadership confrontation, and Pargat was part of the state leadership aligned with Sidhu during that period. Reconciliation would therefore involve not just Amarinder Singh and the Gandhi family, but a state unit whose leadership has changed since he left.It would also raise questions about the position of leaders who remained with Congress through the subsequent elections and organisational changes. Warring's emphasis on youth representation, Pargat's task of consolidating the state unit and Pilot's insistence on collective leadership all point to issues that would need to be addressed.For now, there is no confirmed proposal to bring Captain Amarinder back, no announced role for him and no indication that talks have taken place or are under way.Pilot's "anything is possible" may keep the question open, but the party's immediate task remains to get the current team working together before Punjab votes in 2027.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2021, a car with two flat tires blocked a County Durham farmer’s gate; he flipped it with a telehandler, then a jury cleared him in 2022
articles.summary: A County Durham farmer used a telehandler to flip a car blocking his farm gate, leading to a trial and subsequent acquittal on charges of dangerous driving and criminal damage. Discover the details of the incident, the court proceedings, and the jury's decision in this intriguing rural dispute.
articles.body: A silver Vauxhall Corsa was parked outside Brockersgill Farm in County Durham and became the centre of a criminal trial after farmer Robert Hooper used a telehandler to lift the car and push it onto its side on the road. The vehicle’s driver and passenger had said it could not be moved because it had two deflated tyres, and in February 2022, a jury cleared Hooper of dangerous driving and criminal damage. The incident took place on June 5, 2021, at Newbiggin-in-Teesdale.Hooper is a fourth-generation hill farmer and said that the car blocked access to his property on a busy day on the farm, while the driver, Elliott Johnson, and passenger Charlie Burns had been visiting the area near Low Force waterfall. Hooper told the court that he had asked the men to move the vehicle, but they did not resolve the dispute, which forced him to use a yellow telehandler that was fitted with fork rails to lift the Corsa from the entrance and move it onto the road outside the property. Mobile phone footage played during the trial showed the machine lifting the car, which also showed its forks striking Burns, who was knocked to the ground.The farmer said he felt threatenedHooper was 57 at the time of the trial, and told Durham Crown Court that he had been punched twice by Burns during the confrontation, while also saying that the blows split his lip and that he felt threatened by the two younger men. He also told the court that he had experienced eight break-ins at the farm over the years, and explained that he did not call the police because he had concerns about how quickly officers would arrive.Hooper used the phrase “an Englishman’s home is his castle” to explain his position, and said that he considered the farm entrance to be a part of his property and believed the only way to end the confrontation would be to remove the vehicle. The prosecution and defence disputed how the incident should be understood, with Hooper denying his intention to strike Burns with the telehandler’s forks. Prosecutor David Ward told the jury that the case was not about portraying Hooper as a thug but about whether his actions amounted to dangerous driving and criminal damage. Contemporaneous reporting from ITV News Tyne Tees described the court hearing and the footage presented to jurors, and reported that Hooper had denied both charges and had told the court he had previously asked the men to move the car.A jury cleared him after four days of trialThe case went to trial at Durham Crown Court in early February 2022, and after four days of proceedings, the jury returned not-guilty verdicts on both charges on February 4. The verdict meant that Hooper was acquitted of dangerous driving and criminal damage that arose from the incident, and did not change the fact that he had used the telehandler to move the Corsa, and Burns had been struck by its lifting equipment.The court heard that Johnson and Burns had stopped at the farm entrance because of the car’s two deflated tyres, with the men having been in the area to visit Low Force waterfall, and the blocked access became the source of the dispute. Farmers Weekly reported that the jury cleared Hooper following more than four hours of deliberation, and also reported that Hooper had told the court that he was defending himself and his property after the confrontation. The case attracted attention even beyond the courtroom because of the unusual manner in which the farmer dealt with the parked car, but the legal outcome found Hooper not guilty of the two offences with which he had been charged.You use AI every day. articles.body: BHOPAL: The UK’s Debt Management Office (DMO) has said it can find no evidence that a 109-year-old Indian War Loan, in which a Bhopal merchant invested Rs 35,000 in 1917, was or is an obligation of British govt, leaving a Madhya Pradesh family’s claim unresolved. The office did not say whether the money was repaid.“We have investigated and can find no evidence that the loan you refer to was or is an obligation of the UK govt,” DMO said in an email dated Oct 16.It was replying to Shreyansh Raniwala, legal counsel for the family of Vivek Ruthiya (63) of Sehore.Although the email is not a judicial finding on the family’s claim, and DMO has not acknowledged any outstanding debt, the reply has drawn a sharp reaction from social activist Vinay Ruthiya, who asked why the British authorities had given no account of the loan’s repayment or settlement.Ruthiya said the family had authenticated the available records and sent them through its counsel. He argued that British govt should clarify whether the subscription appears in historical financial records and, if so, how the liability was accounted for.“If the loan was repaid, there should be a record showing when and how it was settled. We submitted the documents they asked for, including the historical certificate. We want a clear answer on what happened to the money,” he said.The family had sought repayment of the Rs 35,000 subscription made to Indian War Loan. It maintains that the amount was never repaid and has been seeking an official account of what became of the investment.The claim rests on a certificate dated June 4, 1917. It records the subscription by Seth Jumma Lal Ruthia of the firm Seth Rama Kishan Jaskaran Ruthia, in the princely state of Bhopal, and bears the signature of W S Davis, then political agent in Bhopal.According to the family, the instrument carried interest at 5.5%, and the certificate has remained among its papers for more than a century.Seth Jumma Lal Ruthia died in 1937, a decade before British rule in India ended.The certificate gives the family a documentary basis for its claim. By itself, however, it does not prove that a debt remains outstanding or that present-day UK govt is legally liable for it. The family estimates that the original sum, compounded at 5.5% a year for 109 years, could run to several crores of rupees today.A calculation based on the rise in gold prices, it suggests, could exceed Rs 10 crore.War loans in British India were govt-issued debt instruments floated to raise funds from the public to finance military expenditure, especially during World War I.Marketed as patriotic investments, they encouraged citizens, traders and institutions to lend money to colonial govt for war efforts including military supplies and troop payments in return for fixed interest.During the British era, a political agent was a key administrative and diplomatic representative of the Crown in princely states.These officers managed relations with local rulers, supervised governance matters and ensured alignment with British authority. Historians also note that W S Davis, who had signed the bond certificate, had literary associations in Bhopal.He apparently had translated Hayat-i-Qudsi: Life of the Nawab Gauhar Begum, a biography written by Sultan Jahan Begum and published in 1918.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhopal | Silver Rate in Bhopal | Bank Holidays in Bhopal | Public Holidays in Bhopal | Petrol Price in Bhopal | Diesel Price in Bhopal | CNG Price in Bhopal | LPG Price in BhopalStay updated with the latest Bhopal news. articles.title: Around 1880, a Delhi author published a rare book with 56 photographic reproductions of portraits of Mughal rulers and royal women; 146 years later, a copy sold in Scotland for £16,640, nearly 21 times its highest estimate
articles.summary: Book published in Delhi around 1880 with 56 Mughal royal portraits sells for £16,640 in Scotland, nearly 21 times its estimate A rare book published in
articles.body: Book published in Delhi around 1880 with 56 Mughal royal portraits sells for £16,640 in Scotland, nearly 21 times its estimateA rare book published in Delhi around 1880, featuring 56 photographic portraits of Mughal rulers and royal women, has sold for £16,640 at an auction in Scotland. The book, which offers a visual record of members of the Mughal dynasty, fetched nearly 21 times its highest estimate, more than 146 years after it was published. According to the official website of UK’s auction house Lyon & Turnbull, the first edition of ‘A History of the Emperors of Delhi in the Mughal Family’ by Munshi Bulaqi Dass was offered as lot 124 in the auction house’s Books and Manuscripts sale on October 1, 2026, in Edinburgh. It had an estimate of £500 to £800 and sold for £16,640.The final price was 20.8 times the upper estimate of £800. The result was also reported by online platform Rare Book Hub, which noted that the book sold as part of the sale of the Indian library of Dr Raj Krishna.56 portraits made from Mughal miniature paintingsThe book contains 56 photographic portraits of male and female members of the Mughal dynasty. According to the auction description, these are albumen-print photographs made from miniature paintings and mounted in the book as originally issued. The portraits are accompanied by lithographic captions, also mounted on the pages. Their mounts feature ornamental borders printed in red, adding a decorative frame to each image.The title describes the subjects as “Shahan and Begmats”, referring to the royal men and women represented in the collection. The book’s combination of photographic reproductions and printed captions makes it a record of how Mughal rulers and royal women were represented in the late 19th century. The volume was printed in Delhi by Mayor Press around 1880. The auction catalogue describes it as a first edition in an original-style black moiré cloth binding decorated with gilt.A rare record of the Mughal dynastyAccording to the official website of the auction house, the book is a “very rare photographic survey” of male and female members of the Mughal dynasty. According to the official listing on the website, no copies had been traced in institutional libraries. As per the website, Bulaqi Dass published another photographic account of earlier Indian rulers, titled ‘Tawarikh-i Ghuri,’ which covered the Ghurid rulers and the Delhi Sultanate. That work was written in Urdu.The title page of ‘A History of the Emperors of Delhi in the Mughal Family’ provides a brief account of the author’s family background. Bulaqi Dass identified himself as the son of the late Rai Juggan Lal, who had served as assistant private secretary in the British Government Agency in Delhi, and the grandson of Rai Sona Mull, a risaldar in the Nizam’s States in Hyderabad, Deccan. These details offer a glimpse into the author’s background, while the book itself preserves a collection of royal portraits through the photographic technology available in the 19th century.From a Delhi publication to a Scottish auctionThe book’s journey from its publication in Delhi around 1880 to its sale in Edinburgh in October 2026 spans more than a century and four decades. Its sale price of £16,640 was substantially higher than the auction house’s estimate of £500 to £800. The result highlights the demand that can exist for rare books documenting India’s royal and cultural history, particularly when they contain extensive visual material. In this case, the volume’s 56 photographic portraits of Mughal rulers and royal women were central to its significance as a historical record. The auction listing also records condition issues, including a repaired tear to the title page and a worn and repaired spine. Despite these defects, the book sold for more than 20 times its highest estimate.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: In 1993, DuPage County began converting an old quarry in Illinois into a reservoir for Salt Creek floodwater threatening communities; the facility can hold 8,300 acre-feet, or about 2.7 billion gallons
articles.summary: Discover how DuPage County turned an old quarry into a crucial flood-control reservoir to protect communities from Salt Creek flooding. Learn about its capacity, history, and operation.
articles.body: DuPage County, Illinois, began converting the former Elmhurst-Chicago Stone quarry into a flood-control facility in March 1993, creating a reservoir designed to store excess water from Salt Creek during periods of high water. According to DuPage County Stormwater Management, the reservoir can hold water up to 8,300 acre-feet, equivalent to approximately 2.7 billion US gallons. After the county purchased the quarry in 1992, the facility became operational in 1996, and it is located south of North Avenue along Illinois Route 83 in Elmhurst.The flood that changed the quarry’s purposeAfter severe flooding in Elmhurst in August 1987, the decisions to acquire the quarry were set in motion. Oak Brook Magazine reported that within the 12 hours on August 13 and 14, 9.5 inches of rain fell, which caused the Salt Creek to rise from its average level of 2.4 feet to 12.85 feet. The resulting consequence included an estimated damage of $33 million at the time, with roads, homes, and businesses being affected.According to the same report, the Elmhurst History Museum recorded more than 50,000 sandbags filled by the Department of Public Works, while the fire department and police department handled 1,745 and 2,000 calls, respectively. Governor Jim Thompson issued a disaster declaration, while President Ronald Reagan authorised federal emergency assistance. In addition, the National Guard and Red Cross had also responded.The Elmhurst History Museum, as cited by Oak Brook Magazine, estimated that the facility had helped save approximately 4,000 homes from flooding. The quarry's earlier industrial history began in 1883, when, during well drilling, limestone was discovered near the surface. The Hammerschmidt family developed the Elmhurst-Chicago Stone Company, which supplied limestone for building foundations and walls. The company later pivoted towards creating ready-mixed concrete from crushed stone, which was used in regional infrastructure, including major expressways. The county's acquisition changed the quarry's function without removing its existing geological structure. Its two excavated sections, known as the east and west lobes, became the principal storage areas in the flood-control system.Inside the quarry’s floodwater systemWhen Salt Creek approaches flood stage, excess water goes through a diversion channel that leads to a drop shaft,then it falls into a 400-foot tunnel beneath Route 83 and enters the west lobe. From that point, the water passes through a rock opening known as the keyway into the east lobe, which has an average depth of 200 feet, with its deepest point reaching 240 feet.A high rock wall separates the two sections and supports West Avenue, except where the keyway lets the water pass between them. A seven-foot-square steel sluice gate controls the diversion of water from Salt Creek, which officials can operate on site or remotely. The system also includes a concrete barrier, known as a weir, over which water can flow when creek levels rise sufficiently.Once stored in the quarry, the water remains there until creek levels recede, after which it is returned to Salt Creek by pumping through an aerating structure. The system is designed to manage the release of stored water at controlled flow rates as part of the wider flood-control operation. The facility also supports flood management beyond Elmhurst as Salt Creek is part of a wider watershed, so managing excess water at the quarry contributes to conditions further downstream. Its role extends beyond storing water within the excavation and may provide a means of managing high flows across a connected system of communities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2018, Steve and Connie Ballmer and the Clippers gave $10 million to restore Los Angeles basketball courts; four years later, the project finished renovations on 350 public courts across the city
articles.summary: In 2018, Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer and his wife, Connie Ballmer, gave $10 million to renovate public basketball courts across Los Angeles.
articles.body: In 2018, Los Angeles Clippers owner Steve Ballmer and his wife, Connie Ballmer, gave $10 million to renovate public basketball courts across Los Angeles. Four years later, the project reached its goal, with 350 courts refurbished across the city. The final renovated court was unveiled on June 28, 2022, at the Michelle and Barack Obama Sports Center in Los Angeles. Ballmer attended the event with then-Mayor Eric Garcetti, marking the completion of the Clippers Community Courts project.The Clippers had partnered with the Los Angeles Parks Foundation to renovate the courts. The Ballmers were initially approached in 2018 to help restore a select number of courts, but they decided to fund renovations across the city.“This was the largest donation ever to the City of Los Angeles’ parks system and it has transformed recreation centers, and been a point of pride, for nearly every neighborhood in the City,” said Carolyn Ramsay, the Los Angeles Parks Foundation’s executive director.Steve Ballmer: Project made basketball more accessibleSteve Ballmer said the project has made basketball courts more accessible to people across Los Angeles.“The City of L.A.'s population is almost 4 (million) people, and 98% of them live within two miles of a Clippers Community Court. That means 3.9 (million) people have access to these courts and all of the benefits that come with them," Ballmer said on Tuesday. "With our partners at the Los Angeles Parks Foundation and L.A.’s Department of Recreation and Parks, this is a proud achievement."The renovated facilities have also served purposes beyond sports. During the Covid-19 pandemic, some were used as shelters, emergency childcare centres and alternative learning sites. Ballmer said the project was aimed at making a difference in the lives of young people. The renovated courts are also expected to support youth sports in Los Angeles ahead of the 2028 Summer Olympics, which the city will host.“impact kids' lives... But if we get a few fans out of it, I’m good with that too," he said. He then added, "We're here to win championships, excite fans and help kids."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2020, scientists poured dye into an Arkansas creek that ran into a dry stretch; they found the missing water resurfacing 2.9 miles farther downstream
articles.summary: Discover how USGS scientists used fluorescent dye to trace water flow in Arkansas's Big Creek, revealing connections between dry and flowing sections in the karst landscape. Explore the implications for water management and conservation.
articles.body: In October 2020, scientists investigating a stream in northwestern Arkansas used fluorescent dye to trace a hydrological connection beneath a seemingly dry stretch of creek. Following the introduction of the dye into a flowing section of the Left Fork of Big Creek, researchers noticed a point 2.9 miles downstream where surface flow resumed. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) spearheaded this field research as part of a targeted project on stream and groundwater interaction in Newton County, Arkansas, releasing the finalised data in January 2022. Moving into 2026, regional water management authorities actively utilise these resulting sub-surface karst maps to implement long-term watershed protection protocols and trace localised aquifer recharge rates.Tracing water through a dry stretchOn October 13 and 14, 2020, the investigation began when USGS researchers examined the Big Creek watershed to identify regions where streams lost or gained water. Primarily, the team focused on Big Creek and the Left Fork of Big Creek, while also examining the tributaries where road access permitted. The team took 13 stream-discharge measurements and recorded 48 observations of zero surface flow during the 28-hour investigation. These observations helped identify losing reaches, where water leaves a stream channel, and gaining reaches, where water enters it.After the initial examination, the team established 27 monitoring regions to detect fluorescent tracer dyes. On October 15, they introduced fluorescein into a flowing section of the Left Fork of Big Creek, upstream of a completely dry reach. Because karst systems feature permanently flooded phreatic conduits deep beneath unsaturated surface gravel packs, this underlying subterranean plumbing network remained active, providing the necessary hydrostatic mechanism to transport the tracer. The dye gave a way to test whether water from the injection area was connected to the locations further downstream. Scientists could then examine monitoring sites for proof of the tracer instead of relying only on the appearance of the creek.The dye was detected 2.9 miles downstream, at the next gaining reach, and at additional monitoring sites farther along the stream. This thus solidified a connection between the injection site and the downstream recovery site. Crucially, while the head-to-head volumetric data did not indicate a 100% quantitative recovery of all lost upstream water molecules, the clear detection of the chemical tracer confirmed a definitive subsurface pathway. Rather, the tracer showed that water from the flowing reach could travel through the local hydrological system and reach the downstream section.Why water disappears in the OzarksBig Creek lies in the Ozark region. Here, limestone formations have developed geological features known as karst, and over time, water dissolves soluble rock, creating fractures, openings and underground conduits. In these landscapes, water can seep out of a stream, move through the subsurface and emerge farther downstream. The USGS identifies the Mississippian-age Boone Formation, a limestone unit underlying substantial sections of Big Creek and the Left Fork, as a geological formation commonly affected by karst processes.Therefore, a dry stream channel does not really mean that all the water has vanished from the wider drainage system. Some water may enter underground pathways and return to the surface elsewhere. Depending on the local geology, it may also travel to a spring, cave or different drainage area. As these underground pathways are not always apparent from surface geography, researchers use fluorescent dye tracing to identify connections between losing and gaining reaches.What the findings mean for water managementIt is essential to understand the interaction between surface water and groundwater in karst areas since the transport of water through the subsurface may be unpredictable. According to the USGS, activities that take place on the surface may impact the quality and quantity of groundwater in such interconnected systems. Identifying where streams lose or regain water can help researchers and resource managers understand how water moves through a watershed and assess potential pathways through which contaminants could travel. Notably, the Big Creek study identified the hydrological connection and was not a test for pollutants.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘We’ve got four little kids, wife never loved politics’: JD Vance says he may skip 2028 presidential race
articles.summary: US Vice President JD Vance has acknowledged that he may not run for president in 2028, saying his wife, second lady Usha Vance, and their four young
articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has acknowledged that he may not run for president in 2028, saying his wife, second lady Usha Vance, and their four young children will be part of the decision as he weighs his political future.“Of course there’s a chance,” Vance said during a CBS News town hall in Michigan, responding to the possibility of sitting out the next presidential election.“We’ve got four little kids; my wife has never loved politics. She loves public service,” Vance said, explaining why his family could play a role in the decision.The vice president said he had not made up his mind about a potential White House bid and described himself as a procrastinator when it comes to major life decisions, the New York Post reported.“The way that I think about life, big life decisions, my wife will tell you this: I’m a procrastinator. I hate thinking about it,” Vance said.Vance also highlighted the demands of his current role, saying he had tried to do as much good as possible as vice president.He indicated that he would give the 2028 question more serious consideration after the November midterm elections, rather than make an early commitment to a presidential campaign.Vance leads early Republican raceVance is widely viewed as an early frontrunner to become the Republican Party's presidential nominee after President Donald Trump. Trump has previously described his vice president as a likely successor, although he has also said it is too early to endorse a candidate for 2028.According to the RealClearPolling average cited by the New York Post, Vance leads Secretary of State Marco Rubio by 15 percentage points in the Republican primary race, with 39 per cent support. Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, follows with 11 per cent.Despite the early polling advantage, Vance has yet to signal whether he intends to seek the presidency. His remarks suggest that family considerations and his current responsibilities could influence his decision.Usha Vance's role in the decisionA presidential campaign would also bring a more prominent political role for Usha Vance, who has previously said that she and her husband do not always agree on political issues.In a March interview with NBC News, Usha said her views sometimes did not fit neatly into traditional political categories.“Sometimes I have thoughts that fit very comfortably into one side or another. Sometimes I have views that are way more idiosyncratic,” she said.She also described herself as a sounding board for her husband rather than someone involved in his political work.“I’m not his staffer. I’m not involved in this in any professional sense,” Usha said, adding that there was no expectation that the couple would agree on everything.The family welcomed its fourth child, a son named Alec, on July 19. The newborn joined the couple's three older children, Ewan, 9, Vivek, 6, and Mirabel, 4.Usha had said in March that a potential 2028 presidential campaign was not yet a priority for the family, with Vance focused on the midterm elections and the responsibilities of his current position.“If you come back in 2027 and ask me, I’ll have a better sense of, you know, what he’s thinking in that way,” she told NBC News.For now, Vance's decision remains open, even as he maintains an early lead over potential Republican rivals in polling for the next presidential election.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2018, New York researchers buried hot-water loops beneath pavement; a small-scale freeze-chamber test showed they could keep the surface of a test section ice-free
articles.summary: Discover how New York researchers are using heated water loops beneath asphalt to prevent icy roads and reduce environmental impact, improving safety during winter storms.
articles.body: New York uses a lot of salt, the standard solution for snowy roadways. A 2018 report says the salt has pushed chloride levels in the state’s freshwater streams up to about a quarter of the concentration in seawater and that the state spends about $1.6 billion a year on roadway deicing. Salt also chews up pavement. For years, engineers have been searching for a more environmentally friendly way of keeping highways clear.One was tested by researchers at Stony Brook University, in collaboration with partners at Columbia University and Cornell University. They built a small section of pavement with loops of warm fluid buried in the gravel base layer under the asphalt and tested it in a freeze chamber. The loops provided enough heat to keep the surface ice-free, although a considerable share of the heat leaked downward, according to the team’s final report, published in April 2018 and archived by the National Transportation Library.Why put the loops under the asphaltHeated pavement is not a new concept. The Netherlands built a system that circulated geothermal fluid through loops in the asphalt layer, and it kept surfaces ice-free through the winter, the report says. But the Dutch design needed a specially formulated crack-resistant asphalt mix and a plastic geogrid to stop stress around the loops from cracking the surface. That pushed up costs and limited its adoption in the US. The Stony Brook researchers relocated the loops into the aggregate foundation layer, under the asphalt, so they could utilise a traditional thin asphalt surface without those concerns. Their whole proposal combines pavement loops with geothermal ground loops along the roadway, circulation pumps and solar panels to power the pumps, which would allow it to operate in isolated locations distant from the grid.In the freeze chamberColumbia University’s project page puts out the team’s two concerns from the beginning. One was structural: the risk of bumps appearing over the loops because pipes and pavement have varying stiffnesses. The other was thermal: maintaining the surface free of ice in very low temperatures and heavy snow.To test the thermal side, the researchers built a stretch of pavement inside an insulated wooden box about 600 millimetres square, according to the report. From the top down it had 100 millimetres of asphalt, 150 millimetres of base, 150 millimetres of subbase and 300 millimetres of subgrade. A single W-shaped loop ran through the middle of the base. A heating device pushed a 50-50 water and propylene glycol mix through it at 31.5 degrees Celsius, which is a warm bath, not anything scalding. The freeze chamber was held at minus 10 degrees Celsius for 48 hours before the fluid was started, by which time the surface had settled at about minus 7.The report says that after around 11 hours, the surface above the entrance and the middle of the loop crossed freezing as the fluid circulated. The fluid reaches the far end cooler, and the surface above the outlet took about 16 hours to cross freezing. Everything settled at about 24 hours, with the surface about 2.5 degrees Celsius above freezing over the entrance, about 1 degree in the centre and about half a degree near the outlet. In a second trial, the scientists put a 25 mm (about 1 inch) layer of ice cubes on the surface before starting the pump, and the surface still climbed above freezing in roughly 10 hours.What the report foundThe report says about 58% of the heat went up and 42% went down into the earth. The authors propose an insulating layer under the loops to drive more heat to the surface. They then modelled the design for Buffalo, New York City and Washington, DC. In New York City, preventing every freezing event would have required 170 watts per metre of loop. The report recommends capping it at 100 watts per metre, which still raised the lowest predicted winter surface temperature in New York City from about minus 12.5 to about minus 6 degrees Celsius.The report is frank about its limitations. The test segment was modest and constructed using a cold patch asphalt mix purchased from a local store and a PVC loop. The authors say PVC would not suit a real road, where HDPE or metal tubing is preferable. The research also revealed the loops would make little difference to how the surface deforms under a tyre. The authors say the idea now needs a full-scale test on a real road with a thicker layer of asphalt to show whether it can keep a long stretch of highway ice-free through an actual winter.You use AI every day. articles.title: After seeing an oil spill in San Francisco Bay, one man walked for 22 years and stayed silent for 17; he later helped write U.S. oil-spill regulations
articles.summary: Explore the incredible 22-year journey of John Francis, who transformed his life after an oil spill in San Francisco Bay, leading to significant contributions in environmental activism and U.S. oil-spill regulations.
articles.body: In 1971, an oil spill in San Francisco Bay prompted John Francis to reconsider his relationship with the environment. He made a commitment to give up motorised transport for travelling on foot, a commitment which endured for 22 years. According to the University of Wisconsin, this collision between the Arizona Standard and the Oregon Standard released a total of 800,000 US gallons of oil into the bay.Francis, who was 26 at the time, joined volunteers responding to the damage and subsequently stopped using cars, buses, and aeroplanes as a personal responsibility to reduce pollution. The decision was met with negative responses from friends and family, which prompted Francis, on his 27th birthday, to stop speaking. Initially, the silence was intended to last one day, but he renewed the commitment after pondering it each year and eventually maintained it for 17 years.Completing his education without motorised transportAccording to the Nelson Institute, Francis pursued his higher education by travelling between universities on foot, and the journeys required covering approximately 350, 800, and 1,400 miles respectively for his bachelor’s, master’s, and doctorate. He received his bachelor's degree from Southern Oregon University, continued with a master's in environmental studies from the University of Montana, and a doctorate in land resources from the University of Wisconsin–Madison.The process of entering university required Francis to move months or years ahead of schedule before the classes began. He supported his education by taking up jobs occasionally and playing his Banjo. The physical effort to make this possible was very demanding; it required Francis to walk around 20 miles a day, which eventually wore out his shoes. On top of the complications, his size 13 feet and limited finances narrowed the options for finding new replacements. Eventually, down the line, he was sponsored by the shoe company Timberland, which provided him with new footwear when needed.His vow of silence did not hinder his ambition to participate in academic life, and before he started his doctorate, Francis assured his professors that his personal commitment would not affect his studies. Later, he credited listening to lectures and fellow students for helping him understand environmental issues. Subsequently, he also founded a nonprofit organisation called Planetwalk, an effort that promoted environmental awareness through international friendship, newsletters, films, and other publications.From environmental activism to public serviceAfter Francis completed his doctorate, he travelled to Washington, DC, and joined the United States Coast Guard Oil Pollution Act of 1990 Staff. He worked there in the capacity of project manager and assisted in writing regulations for oil spills. Eventually, in 1991, he was appointed as the Goodwill Ambassador to the World’s Grassroots Communities by the United Nations Environment Programme.Subsequently, he continued his environmental education work through public speaking and writing, publishing The Planetwalker: 17 Years of Silence, 22 Years of Walking and The Ragged Edge of Silence: Finding Peace in a Noisy World. Later, through the years, Francis reconsidered his decision not to use motorised transport, calling it very limiting and akin to a prison. The realisation dawned on him in 1994, while travelling in Venezuela on a journey through South America, prompting him to fly to see his parents, who had not seen him in years. Recalling the experience, Francis said to the Nelson Institute for Environmental Studies, “They were freaked out, but overjoyed because they thought they would never see me again,”.Francis’s philosophy is to bridge the gap between human welfare and environmental conservation; he believes the way humans treat one another is reflected in the environment. In April 2025, the Nelson Institute reported that Francis had begun a walk across Africa, covering a planned distance of approximately 6,000 miles, at the age of 79.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1997, Beach Boys co-founder Mike Love built a Lake Tahoe home on 2.5 acres; nearly 30 years later, the $43 million estate is for sale after he protected another six surrounding acres from development
articles.summary: Some luxury homes are defined by what they offer. Others stand out for what they leave untouched.
articles.body: Some luxury homes are defined by what they offer. Others stand out for what they leave untouched. At Mike Love’s sprawling Lake Tahoe retreat, the appeal extends beyond the sweeping Sierra Nevada views, expansive glass walls and private leisure spaces. The Beach Boys co-founder has also taken steps to preserve the natural landscape surrounding his home, placing six additional acres under conservation protection to guard against future development. Now, nearly three decades after the property was built, the estate is entering a new chapter, with a $43 million asking price, states an online report by People.A retreat shaped by its surroundingsIf we go by the exclusive report by People, Love, 85, built the three-storey residence in 1997 on a 2.5-acre plot in Incline Village, Nevada, near Lake Tahoe’s northeastern shore. He and his wife, Jacquelyne Piesen, spent more than four decades at the property, which became a private retreat for their family and a setting for much of the musician’s creative work.And according to Morning Star report, the home’s connection to its surroundings is evident in its construction, with stone sourced directly from the property incorporated throughout the residence. Beyond the main grounds, the couple also worked with organisations including the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency and the University of California, Davis, on efforts to protect the lake’s water quality and natural environment.The decision to place six neighbouring acres under conservation protection further reflects that commitment, preserving surrounding pine trees and wildlife from development, states People report.Inside the $43 million estateThe property, listed in April 2026, offers 10 bedrooms, 12 full bathrooms and three half-bathrooms. Its main living area centres on a generous great room, where floor-to-ceiling glass and retractable doors open onto a terrace overlooking the lake, adds the online report.The kitchen and dining spaces are similarly oriented towards the water, making the views an integral part of everyday living rather than a backdrop reserved for special occasions.Eight en-suite bedrooms are spread across three floors, with several featuring private balconies. The primary suite occupies a separate wing, offering two bathrooms, a soaking tub, a steam room, a sun deck and a private coffee bar, explains the online report too.Outside, the amenities are designed for both entertaining and family life. A swimming pool and 10-person hot tub sit alongside a custom trampoline and playground, while the upper lawn has also accommodated a temporary ice-skating rink.With Love’s eight children now grown up, the family has decided to put the long-held residence on the market. The listing is being handled by Jeannette Harpole of Keller Williams Everett, adds the report.A longstanding environmental commitmentAs per Morning Star, Love’s interest in conservation extends beyond his private property. In 2012, he attended the dedication of Lake Tahoe’s first highway roundabout, a $2.4 million project intended to improve road safety while helping protect the lake’s renowned clarity and incorporating local public art, claims the online report.Environmental awareness has also surfaced in his musical work. The Beach Boys’ song Don’t Go Near the Water addressed pollution and the need to treat the natural world with greater care, adds People report.As the Incline Village estate seeks a new owner, its conservation measures remain a distinctive part of its story. articles.title: A man who came to Britain from Barbados at age 12 has lived in the UK for 50 years, but at 62 he still faces deportation because of a past criminal conviction and a legal dispute over his immigration status
articles.summary: A 62-year-old London resident who moved to Britain from Barbados 50 years ago remains caught in legal uncertainty as the Home Office continues trying to
articles.body: A 62-year-old London resident who moved to Britain from Barbados 50 years ago remains caught in legal uncertainty as the Home Office continues trying to deport him because of a past criminal conviction. Tony Hall arrived in the UK in 1976, aged 12, to join his family. Despite living in the country for 50 years, he has spent the past 14 years on a government deportation list. This status means he cannot work, rent a home, claim state benefits or open a bank account. According to a report by The Guardian, Hall's case shows that problems linked to the Windrush scandal remain unresolved. Thousands of Caribbean migrants and their descendants have received official documents confirming their right to live in Britain. However, Hall still faces deportation to an island where he has no surviving relatives and no memories of adult life.Past conviction and a double penaltyHall's immigration problems began with a 2001 conviction for conspiracy to rob and possession of a firearm with intent. He received an eight-year prison sentence after planning a security van robbery with friends. Hall carried a toy gun during the incident, although a real firearm was also found in the vehicle before the crime took place. After completing his prison sentence, he was moved straight into immigration detention. In January 2010, Home Office officials put him on a flight to Barbados. However, border officials in Barbados refused to let him enter because he had been away for decades. He was sent back to London on the same plane the next day.In an interview with The Guardian, Hall admitted that he had made mistakes in the past. However, he pointed out that he had served the prison sentence ordered by the court. “When I was young I was a bit of a tearaway; I was a pain. Once you get into trouble, it's hard to get out,” Hall told The Guardian. “I've paid the price. I've grown up a bit.” His legal supporters argue that keeping him under the threat of deportation for years amounts to a second punishment. They say this stops him from rebuilding his life in the country where he grew up and went to school.Decades of mandatory reporting requirementsSince being released from immigration detention in 2012, Hall has had to report to a Home Office centre every two weeks. The journey takes two hours and involves several trips on London's Overground and Underground rail networks. He must then take a bus and wait in a queue to show his documents. Hall estimates that he has made this journey more than 350 times over the past 14 years. Every visit brings the risk of sudden arrest and transfer to an immigration removal centre. “Sometimes I feel mad at them,” Hall told The Guardian about his dealings with reporting centre staff. “I tell them: 'I've been here for 50 years.' They say: 'That's not my department. We're not here to do your case.'” While Hall was in prison, his local council cleared his flat and threw away his personal belongings. As a result, he no longer has important documents from his past. Without valid papers from either the UK or Barbados, he is effectively stateless.Roots of the Windrush administrative crisisHall first came to London as the youngest child of a Barbadian mother who had moved to Britain to work in a gin factory. His stepfather worked as a mechanic for British Rail. His five older sisters had moved to London earlier and successfully obtained British citizenship in the 1970s. However, Hall was later placed in local authority care as a teenager. Social workers failed to officially record his immigration status at the time. This mistake left his legal position unresolved when immigration laws became stricter in later decades. Barrister Martin Forde, who designed the official Windrush compensation scheme in 2019, told The Guardian that many people with complicated histories or criminal records remain trapped in long-running government delays. “Compassion is not exactly their middle name,” Forde told The Guardian, referring to the Home Office. “My strong suspicion is that there are many of these cases; many will be people of no fixed abode who won't want to put their head above the parapet.” Forde added that trying to remove people who have lived in the country for many years, after they have already served their criminal sentences, “goes against a sense of fairness.”Uncertain future and threat of homelessnessOfficial figures show that more than 18,000 people have received documents confirming their right to stay in the UK through government Windrush schemes set up since 2018. More than £132m has also been paid in compensation to people affected by the scandal. However, campaigners say cases involving people with past criminal convictions often remain unresolved. Hall currently depends on his sister, who works with children with special needs for a London council, for a place to stay. However, she plans to move house soon. This leaves Hall facing the immediate risk of becoming homeless unless his immigration status is settled.Hall's sister spoke to The Guardian anonymously to protect her job. She expressed anger at the way her brother had been treated during years of uncertainty. “I can't help but feel angry for him. They've treated him so badly, wasting 14 years of his life, keeping him in limbo,” she told The Guardian. “He made a mistake; he got caught up with the wrong people and he was sentenced. But he's done the time, paid the penalty, and now he wants to be able to live a normal life, to be able to work.” With no change to his deportation order, Hall continues to report to the Home Office every two weeks. He remains uncertain whether government ministers will use their powers to make an exception in his case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘No specific period prescribed’: Rijiju writes to Kharge on delay in proroguing Monsoon Session
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju on Monday responded to Congress president and Rajya Sabha LoP Mallikarjun Kharge, who wrote to Prime Minister
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju on Monday responded to Congress president and Rajya Sabha LoP Mallikarjun Kharge, who wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi flagging the “unusual delay” in proroguing the Monsoon Session of Parliament, which ended on August 13 but has yet to be formally prorogued.Also Read | 'Don't try to bulldoze another Constitutional Amendment Bill': Kharge writes to PM Modi"With regard to your observation that Parliament has not been prorogued even though 64 days have passed since the House was adjourned sine die on August 13, I would like to clarify that there is no constitutional requirement prescribing a specific period within which a House must be prorogued following its adjournment sine die," Rijiju, the parliamentary affairs minister, wrote in his letter to Kharge."The mere fact that a House has not been prorogued during such an interval does not, by itself, give rise to any constitutional or procedural impropriety," he added.The minister also cited several instances of similar delays during the Congress-led UPA government, inclduing once in 2008, when Houses took up to 87 days to be prorogued.Rijiju further addressed Kharge’s claim regarding the Constitutional Amendment Bill on delimitation. He said the government had reached out to the Congress, the principal opposition party, several times but approached other opposition parties after the Congress failed to provide dates for a discussion."I wrote to you on March 16, March 26 and April 12 in this regard. I had also discussed the matter with you personally and sought your support and cooperation. I also met Shri Rahul Gandhi, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, to discuss the issue and seek his cooperation. However, despite repeated requests, the Congress party did not provide dates for discussion, following which the government reached out to other political parties," he wrote.Citing this, Rijiju expressed surprise that the demand for consultation was still being raised repeatedly and called for the opposition's "constructive cooperation" rather than a "repetition" of the "same demand."Underlining the government’s “firm willingness” to hold consultations, Rijiju reiterated its commitment to the basic principles of parliamentary democracy and expressed hope that the Congress would play a “constructive role” and not obstruct “important future legislations."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2017, nearly 90-year-old Don Doll protected his 186-acre Michigan farm forever so his six children would not split the land he shared with his late wife
articles.summary: In 2017, nearly 90-year-old Don Doll secured a conservation easement for his 186-acre Michigan farm to prevent his six children from dividing the land, preserving it for future generations. Discover how this move protects agricultural land and maintains family legacy.
articles.body: Don Doll was almost 90 years old when he secured permanent protection for his 186-acre Michigan farm in 2017 because he was worried that his six children might have to divide the property after his death. Doll and his late wife, Therese, had raised all six children on the land, which had remained in the same family for more than 150 years, and had owned the property since 1962, according to Legacy Land Conservancy’s account of the farm’s protection. It sits off Heim Road near Chelsea in Washtenaw County and includes rolling fields, woodland, and wetlands.“I kept thinking the farm was going to get split up if it went to six kids,” Doll said in the account. “And it would have to be all six; I don’t play favorites.” He decided after learning about conservation easements that the arrangement provided a way to protect the farm without having to choose which child might receive which part.The agreement restricts future developmentThe farm was protected through Washtenaw County’s Natural Areas Preservation Program, and Legacy Land Conservancy provided support during negotiations and completion of the easement. A conservation easement places legally binding restrictions on how land can be developed, and the landowner retains ownership but gives up certain development rights under the agreement. Michigan’s Department of Agriculture and Rural Development explains that agricultural conservation easements can restrict subdivision and non-agricultural development permanently while keeping land in private ownership.The arrangement addressed a specific concern about inheritance, since passing a farm to six children could have divided the property into smaller parcels, and the easement protects the land against development covered by its terms, regardless of who owns it in the future. The property does not automatically become public, and Michigan’s guidance states that a conservation easement does not, by itself, require public access since owners can continue using their land within the restrictions that are set out in the agreement.The county programme keeps farmland in private handsWashtenaw County’s Natural Areas Preservation Program buys conservation easements so that they can restrict development without requiring landowners to sell their property, and the programme considers agricultural soil quality, development pressure and links to existing protected land, according to Legacy Land Conservancy. The agreement made sure that Don Doll's 186-acre farm remained privately owned while limiting future development, and Legacy Land Conservancy helped facilitate the protection through its work with the county’s parks and recreation commission. Michigan also has a state-level framework for agricultural conservation easements that restrict non-farm development and also allow private ownership to continue.The farm connects to other protected landThe Doll property had an impressive location and agricultural value, and Legacy Land Conservancy reported that the farm had high-quality soil, faced development pressure, and adjoined other protected land, with its easement connecting two existing conservation easements. The farm also lies about a quarter-mile from more than 400 additional acres of contiguous protected land, including Goose Lake State Game Area and Washtenaw County Parks and Recreation Commission’s Koenn Preserve, according to the conservancy’s 2017 account.The US Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service describes its Agricultural Conservation Easement Program as a source of financial and technical assistance for eligible partners who are working to conserve agricultural land and wetlands, and the programme’s agricultural land easements limit non-agricultural uses while keeping farms in production. Legacy’s account does not identify the exact division of funding for Doll’s easement or provide a detailed schedule of restrictions for the property, but it does state that Washtenaw County’s programme purchased the farmland conservation easement and that Legacy helped negotiate and complete it. Doll was still active on the farm when the protection was announced in 2017, and at nearly 90, he said that he wanted the property to stay exactly the way it was. The agreement put permanent development restrictions in place while keeping the farm in private hands.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
