articles.title: Meet Anand Kumar: He helped his mother sell papads after losing his Cambridge dream; today, his Super 30 inspires underprivileged IIT aspirants
articles.summary: He started his journey with only Rs 500 and two students in a tiny rented classroom in Patna, Bihar.
articles.body: He started his journey with only Rs 500 and two students in a tiny rented classroom in Patna, Bihar. A young mathematics enthusiast started teaching students with nothing but passion for numbers and power of education. Though there was no grand institute, no money and of course no guarantee of success. But it didn’t stop him from pursuing a noble cause.Years ago, what started as a teaching initiative eventually grew into Super 30, a programme that helped economically disadvantaged students prepare for admission to India’s prestigious Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs).Meet Anand KumarMeet Anand Kumar whose journey began from a rented classroom costing Rs 500 a month to receiving a Padma Shri in 2023 for his professional achievement which didn’t come to him easily. He was recoginsed by the Government of India for his contribution to education by conferring the Padma Shri on him in the Literature and Education category.His love for mathematicsAnand was born on January 1, 1973, in Patna, Bihar. He grew up in a family that could not afford the privileges enjoyed by financially comfortable students. His father, Rajendra Prasad, was a clerk in the postal department and he studied at a Hindi-medium government school.Maths was his love and it became his passion early in life. Even when resources were limited, he continued to study the subject. As a student, he wrote papers on number theory that were published in international mathematical journals.The death of Cambridge dreamsFor a young man fascinated by mathematics, the possibility of studying at the University of Cambridge was a major opportunity. He was able to get an admission there in the 1990s. However, life had other plans. During that time, his father died, and the family's financial burden came on him. And with that went away his Cambridge dream because the cost of pursuing higher education was simply too much.Later, to help make ends meet, Kumar helped his mother, Jayanti Devi, sell papads. But he continued to study mathematics. He knew what it meant to have the ability to pursue a dream but lacked the financial means to do so. And because he himself went through such financial issues, he knew exactly what it meant for a student.From two students to a classroom full of dreamsIn 1992, he established the Ramanujan School of Mathematics as a mathematics club. He was still in college at that time. He started giving free lessons to two students before the growing demand for his teaching led him to charge fees.Then came a student for IIT-JEE preparation but could not afford the fees. Now this was the turning point which gave Kumar the idea for which he is known worldwide.Formation of Super 30The idea behind Super 30 was simple but ambitious. Each year, 30 meritorious students from economically weak backgrounds were selected for the IIT entrance examinations. Anand would provide them study materials, food and accommodation along with coaching and no fee.For thousands of aspirational students, this was their opportunity.The programme was developed under the Ramanujan School of Mathematics, with Kumar's brother, Pranav Kumar, who looked after the management. His mother also played a part in the family-run effort. She would cook for the students.And the rest is history. For Kumar, the idea was rooted in his own experience.Recognition beyond Bihar and IndiaHis effort earned him national as well as global attention. In 2010, Time magazine included Super 30 in its list of the Best of Asia. His story reached a wider audience in 2019 with the release of the Hindi film Super 30, starring Hrithik Roshan as Kumar.The journey that began in a Rs 500 rented classroom had taken a much bigger shape. While Kumar's own dream of being a Cambridge student remained unfulfilled, he built a programme around the belief that financial lets define a student’s opportunity.You use AI every day. articles.title: Manipur on boil again: 3 killed by militants; locals place bodies in front of CM's house
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Three people were killed and three others injured after suspected militants ambushed firewood collectors along the Imphal East-Kangpokpi
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three people were killed and three others injured after suspected militants ambushed firewood collectors along the Imphal East-Kangpokpi district border in Manipur on Monday.The attack triggered protests in Imphal, where locals placed two of the victims' bodies outside Manipur chief minister Y Khemchand Singh's residence.The attack took place around 7am in Khongbal Sunurok Uyok in Kangpokpi district, near Nongshum village in Imphal East. Three people remained missing after the incident, officials said. The protests also led to road blockades and the closure of markets and shops across Imphal.Firewood collectors ambushed in the hillsThe victims were among 16 people who had gone to the hills near their village to collect firewood when suspected militants opened fire on them, officials said.The deceased were identified as Arubam Ronil, 35, Lairenlakpam Inaobi, 51, and Kshetrimayum Sushil, 32. Ronil and Inaobi died on the spot, while Sushil succumbed to his injuries at a private hospital in Imphal, an official said.The injured were identified as N Suraj, 19, Meisnam Somendro, 53, and K Bosan, 45. They were undergoing treatment. Three people were still unaccounted for, news agency PTI reported, citing officials.An injured survivor, who was taken to a private hospital in Imphal, said, "While we were loading the firewood, we were suddenly fired upon."Bodies placed outside CM's residenceAngry locals brought two of the deceased's bodies to Imphal and placed them outside the main gate of the chief minister's residence in Babupara to protest the continuing violence in the state.Police fired several rounds of tear gas shells to disperse the protesters. The bodies were subsequently taken to the Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences (JNIMS).Security was tightened around the chief minister's bungalow and along the routes leading to it.Following the demonstration, Khemchand Singh visited the injured people receiving treatment at a private hospital in Imphal but did not respond to media queries.Protests spread, markets and shops shutThe attack triggered demonstrations at several locations in the state capital. Protesters blocked a road at Khurai Lamlong, while a group of women staged a demonstration at Ema Keithel market.Markets and shops across Imphal shut following the incident, as anger grew over the latest attack.Manipur grappling with violence since 2023The attack on firewood collectors came amid other incidents of violence reported in Manipur over the weekend.In a separate incident, at least 15 houses belonging to the Kuki community were torched in Chassad village in Kamjong district late on Saturday night, officials said on Sunday. Suspected militants allegedly set the houses on fire, forcing several civilians to flee to forest areas and a nearby Army camp.PTI reported that a Kuki civilian was killed and four others sustained bullet injuries when suspected militants attacked the village earlier on Sunday.Deputy chief minister Nemcha Kipgen condemned the violence in Chassad, expressed grief over the death and concern for the injured village leaders and displaced families. She described the burning of houses as an intolerable crime and said she had directed the district administration, state police and security forces to remain vigilant round the clock, protect civilians and their property, and ensure those responsible were brought to justice.Police said a joint team of the Assam Rifles, Border Security Force and Kamjong Police had been deployed in the affected area to bring the situation under control.In another separate incident at Kamjong district headquarters on Saturday night, three Tangkhul Naga civilians sustained bullet injuries when rival armed groups belonging to another community attacked the village.Manipur has been grappling with prolonged violence since May 2023. The latest attack on firewood collectors and the protests that followed came against the backdrop of fresh incidents involving arson, civilian deaths and gunshot injuries in other parts of the state.(With inputs from agencies)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'This wasn't an accident': Australian PM Anthony Albanese says MP Helen Haines was hit in 'deliberate act', motive unclear
articles.summary: Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines was critically injured after being struck by a car outside her electoral office in Victoria state on Monday
articles.body: Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines was critically injured after being struck by a car outside her electoral office in Victoria state on Monday in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described as an apparently deliberate attack.The driver was arrested at the scene.The 65-year-old was hit by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta in the mid-afternoon, police said. She was taken to hospital with critical injuries.“This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is,” Albanese told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).The national counterterrorism team, which brings together police and intelligence agencies, was investigating the incident, the prime minister said.Police said the 43-year-old driver was detained by a passerby before being arrested. A knife was found and seized from inside the vehicle.“A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota,” police said. “At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act.”The motive has not been established, Albanese said.Who is Helen Haines?Haines has represented the rural electorate of Indi, north of Melbourne, since entering parliament in 2019.According to Reuters, her election made history as the first time an independent politician succeeded another independent in the same seat, taking over from Cathy McGowan.Before entering politics, Haines spent three decades working in rural healthcare as a nurse, midwife and academic. She also completed a doctoral thesis on childbirth at Sweden's Uppsala University.She entered parliament through the community movement Voices for Indi, which challenged the traditional conservative stronghold in 2019.During her time in parliament, Haines has championed climate action and regional housing and worked with the ruling Labor government to establish a National Anti-Corruption Commission.Albanese praised her contribution to parliament and her work for her community.“She's someone who is very passionate about her community. She's someone who's not shy about coming forward about what she thinks that community needs, but she's also someone who plays a role in the parliament,” he told ABC.The prime minister also described Haines as “a thoroughly decent, respectful human being who is a delight to work with”.In a statement, Haines' family said she was receiving medical care and thanked bystanders, healthcare workers and police for their assistance. The family and her staff said they would make no further comment at the time and requested privacy.Attack raises concerns over lawmakers' safetyThe incident has renewed concerns about the safety of Australian politicians, who have traditionally been accessible to the public and often carried out their duties without security officers present.Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the preceding three years. Home affairs minister Tony Burke said on Monday that police data recorded more than 1,000 threats against politicians during the 2025-2026 financial year.Albanese said the increasingly polarised political climate had already prompted changes to security arrangements for lawmakers.“I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement,” he told ABC, adding that social media was also playing a role.Australian Federal Police had established a dedicated team the previous year to investigate groups and individuals targeting lawmakers.You use AI every day. articles.title: Anonymous donor leaves rare banknotes at Edinburgh British Heart Foundation charity shop; collection sells for nearly $115,000 at auction
articles.summary: A charity shop donation in Edinburgh has become an unexpected headline.
articles.body: A charity shop donation in Edinburgh has become an unexpected headline. An anonymous donor left albums of rare banknotes at a British Heart Foundation shop, and staff initially didn't know what they were holding. After specialists took a closer look, the collection went to auction and raised $114,434. The sale included a note with a portrait of a young Queen Elizabeth, plus rare notes from Iraq and Saudi Arabia. Read on to learn who spotted the potential, what collectors paid, why the auction house gave up its fee, and where the money goes.How an anonymous donor's albums of rare banknotes reached a British Heart Foundation shop in EdinburghThe story began with a quiet drop-off. The banknotes arrived at the charity's Edinburgh store tucked inside a series of albums, with employees initially unaware of their potential significance. The donor remained anonymous, and the shop, which sits at Straiton Retail Park, had nothing obvious to suggest what the albums contained. According to People, the collection included nearly 160 lots of rare banknotes from countries around the world. Noonans, the London auction house that later sold them, published a press release about the sale on Thursday, October 15, one day after the auction took place. Taken together, those details describe a donation that looked ordinary at first glance but carried an enormous amount of collectable history inside its pages.Why shop staff who did not know the banknotes' value sent the collection to an eBay team in LeedsCuriosity set the process in motion. Shop manager David McCormack said in the Noonans press release, as reported by People, that he and his colleagues looked through the folders but did not know much about the banknotes, so they sent them to the charity's eBay team in Leeds to investigate. When the team uncovered their potential value, McCormack said, everyone was flabbergasted. After recognising that the collection deserved a closer look, the charity turned to Noonans to handle the sale. That chain of decisions, from a puzzled shop team to an online selling team in Leeds and then to an auction house in London, is what allowed the albums to reach collectors who understood exactly what they were looking at.What the nearly 160 lots achieved at auction, from a young Queen Elizabeth note to an Iraqi colour trialThe sale took place on Wednesday, October 14, the collection sold for $114,434, raised for the charity. Among the highlights was an uncirculated banknote with a portrait of a young Queen Elizabeth, issued by the Board of Commissioners of Currency Malaya and British Borneo. Other notable pieces included an extremely rare 1947 Iraqi 10-dinar colour trial and a specimen 100-riyal note from Saudi Arabia dating back to 1961. Andrew Pattison, head of the banknotes department at Noonans, said in the release that the notes attracted collectors from around the world, with many selling for higher prices than expected. That global interest explains how a donation of paper delivered to a retail park shop ended up commanding a six-figure sum in United States dollars.Why Noonans waived its seller's commission and how charitable sales encourage collectors to pay a little moreTwo details help explain the strong result. First, Noonans noted that it waived its seller's commission, which allowed more of the proceeds to go toward the British Heart Foundation's efforts to fund research into heart and circulatory diseases. Second, Pattison said in the release that material of this quality is extremely rare and that collectors responded extremely well, with many notes selling for a little more than normal because of the charitable nature of the sale. In other words, generosity appears to have been truly contagious: the donor gave the collection, the auction house gave up its fee, and bidders were willing to pay slightly above usual levels, all of which pushed more money towards the cause of heart research.Why checking unfamiliar donations before pricing them can turn an anonymous gift into heart research fundingThe broader lesson is straightforward. The Edinburgh team did not pretend to know more than it did. Instead of guessing a price, staff sent the albums onward for investigation, which, according to People, led the charity to Noonans. For anyone clearing out an attic or sorting inherited collections, the story suggests that old banknotes and similar collectables may be worth showing to a specialist before they are given away or sold cheaply. Noonans, for its part, handled the sale of nearly 160 lots and waived its seller's commission, showing how charities and specialists can work together. It also shows why charity shop workers who ask questions can transform a mystery donation into meaningful support.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A rare barn owl family nested in a Manhattan water tower near Central Park, drawing nightly crowds to see a nest experts say is the first on record
articles.summary: A rare nesting of barn owls in a Manhattan water tower near Central Park has drawn crowds of bird-watchers and photographers, marking the first documented instance in the city. Learn more about this unique occurrence and the owls' status.
articles.body: A family of barn owls has made a water tower atop a building on Manhattan’s Upper West Side their residence, and has been drawing bird-watchers and photographers to West 75th Street near Central Park, with ornithologists saying that it is the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in recorded history.Upper West Side resident Elisabeth Williams reported seeing several birds around the tower on October 6, 2026, which is when the owls came to wider public attention. Andrew Farnsworth, who is a migration ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, told the Associated Press that birders had no previous record of a barn owl nest in Manhattan.Bird-watchers have counted at least five young owlsDavid Barrett, a Manhattan birder who runs the Manhattan Bird Alert account, said that he had seen at least one adult owl and five fledglings at the water tower, and had also observed an adult carrying rodents back to the site. Two adults are believed to be present, while some photographers have reported seeing at least six fledglings. The nest has drawn nightly crowds, which include people who had never actively watched birds before, and residents and photographers gather around dusk to view the owls when they leave for hunting. One local resident, Thomas Obersteiner, has also let photographers watch from his roof deck, and told the Associated Press that about 20 people had gathered there on one night. Barn owls are nocturnal, which makes them difficult to spot, and their pale faces and distinctive calls can make them conspicuous when they appear in an urban setting. Their usual nesting sites include barns, other buildings, and suitable cavities.Barn owls are rare across New York StateThe New York State Department of Environmental Conservation says that the American barn owl is rare across the state and has sharply declined over recent decades. New York lies near the northern edge of the bird’s range, and the agency’s 2024 species status assessment identifies open habitats such as grasslands, marshes and agricultural areas as breeding environments for barn owls, who also use cavities in barns and other buildings, cliff crevices and artificial nest boxes. The first New York Breeding Bird Atlas that covered 1980 to 1985 recorded barn owls in 126 survey blocks, and the second atlas, which covered 2000 to 2005, recorded them in 28 blocks. The survey blocks measure where a species was recorded, not the total number of individual owls.Most known nesting areas in New York are on Long Island and Staten Island, according to the state assessment, so a family breeding on the Upper West Side is therefore unusual according to regular urban standards, although just the sighting alone does not establish why the birds chose the water tower or whether they will return.Residents heard the owls before they saw themA few weeks before the nest became widely known, neighbours noticed strange screeching sounds, and Williams and her husband heard intermittent calls beginning in early September. Obersteiner said that he heard wailing noises for two or three weeks in mid-September but did not know they came from owls.Farnsworth told the Associated Press that barn owls use their screeches to communicate, and several residents initially mistook the sounds for a person in distress. The owls’ presence has since attracted people to the block most evenings, and their longer-term status at the site remains unclear; the available reports do not establish whether the family will remain in the tower after the young birds leave the nest.You use AI every day. articles.body: As France reels from violent protests, visuals of seemingly unfazed residents going about their daily routines have also drawn attention on social media, offering a striking contrast to the scenes of rioting, arson and looting across the country.One visual shows a couple calmly sipping their drinks at an outdoor table near the Arc De Triomphe in central Paris, seemingly undisturbed by the unrest around them.Another video, shared by ABC News, shows a jogger continuing her run directly through the crowd of rioters.A determined jogger was seemingly unfazed by the ongoing rioting in Paris as she opted to run directly through the chaos on Saturday. articles.title: In 2021, brothers Tom and Jim Irwin put a permanent easement on their 158-acre Michigan farm, honoring their late father's wish and keeping developers from splitting it
articles.summary: In April 2021, Tom and Jim Irwin placed a permanent conservation easement on their 158-acre family farm in Grass Lake, Michigan, fulfilling their late father's wishes and protecting the land from future development.
articles.body: A permanent conservation easement was placed by brothers Tom and Jim Irwin on their 158-acre family farm in Grass Lake, Michigan, in April 2021, which restricts the property from future development and keeps it together as farmland, forest, and wetlands, and fulfills a wish that their late father, Richard “Dick” Irwin, had already acted on during his lifetime. The farm had been in the Irwin family for more than 150 years, with Tom and Jim inheriting it in 2017. Their father had previously worked with Legacy Land Conservancy to protect another portion of the property through conservation easements between 2004 and 2008, and the brothers completed the new agreement with the Ann Arbor-based nonprofit on Earth Day in 2021, according to Legacy Land Conservancy’s announcement on April 26, 2021.The agreement restricts development but leaves the farm in private handsA conservation easement is a legally binding agreement that places a limit on how land can be developed or used, and it can protect agricultural soil, wetlands, and other natural features without transferring ownership to a government agency or conservation group. The property remains privately owned under the Irwin agreement, but development that would potentially undermine its conservation value is restricted. Michigan’s Department of Agriculture and Rural Development explains that agricultural conservation easements can limit subdivision and other development while making sure that the land is under private ownership, and the restrictions are intended to preserve farmland and open space over the long term.The Irwin property includes rolling farmland, forest, and wetlands off Grass Lake Road, with Legacy saying that the land was at risk of development and sits next to other protected properties in the Sharon Short Hills area. The farm is also part of a roughly 300-acre natural greenway in the area, which supports wildlife habitat and water quality.The farm dates back to an 1836 land purchaseJames Irwin, the brothers’ great-great-great-grandfather, purchased the first 80 acres of the estate in 1836, and the original deeds were signed by President Martin Van Buren on sheepskin, according to Legacy Land Conservancy. At its largest, the farm covered about 354 acres, and later passed through generations of the family. Dick Irwin arranged conservation protection for part of the land before his sons inherited the farm, with Tom and Jim then choosing to place the remaining 158-acre property under a new easement. In comments published by Legacy, the brothers said that their father had taught them to leave the Earth in better condition for the next generation, and they said that the agreement put his values into practice and would keep the farm as one parcel that would extend beyond their lifetimes.Conservation groups helped finance the dealLegacy worked with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service, the Washtenaw County Parks and Recreation Commission, the Carls Foundation, and private contributors to assemble funding for the easement, and the arrangement paid the brothers for the development rights that they agreed to give up. The brothers planned to use part of the proceeds to reinvest in the property, and at the time of the agreement, they leased out the farmland with the intention of restoring the historic barn and farmhouse and restarting the family’s farming business together.Legacy Land Conservancy, founded in 1971, works to protect farmland, natural areas and freshwater resources in the region, and a report in the local Manchester Mirror on May 24, 2021 documented the agreement and the property’s history. The easement does not make the farm public property, since the Irwin family retains ownership, while the conservation restrictions limit future development under the terms of the agreement.You use AI every day.
